title: Cause and effect or just association
subtitle: Evaluating statistical claims: Observational studies and experiments

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: This pattern appears rarely. Learn to recognise it, but do not spend a session on it.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The stem describes either an experiment in which subjects were randomly assigned to treatment groups, or a study in which the researcher only recorded what people already did.
- The choices use words like 'causes', 'is associated with', 'improves' and 'is related to', often paired with different populations.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Ask whether the subjects were randomly assigned to conditions.
- If yes, a cause-and-effect conclusion is allowed.
- If no, only an association is allowed.
- 2) Ask whether they were randomly selected from a population.
- That decides how far the conclusion can be generalized.
- 3) Choose the answer that gets both parts right.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You accept a causal claim from observational data because the correlation looks strong.
Or you mix up the two kinds of randomness: random selection lets you generalize, random assignment lets you claim a cause, and a correct answer can't claim one without having it.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You accept a causal claim from observational data because the correlation looks strong.
Or you mix up the two kinds of randomness: random selection lets you generalize, random assignment lets you claim a cause, and a correct answer can't claim one without having it.
